metadata.description: Worked steps, progressive hints and reviewed follow-up questions.

matches.rationale: Both distinguish repeated quadratic roots from distinct inputs and avoid duplicate counting. The original has two fixed quadratic branches after hidden-square substitution; the candidate additionally classifies a parameter and checks overlap with a linear factor.
sharedKnowledge: Both distinguish repeated quadratic roots from distinct inputs and avoid duplicate counting. The original has two fixed quadratic branches after hidden-square substitution; the candidate additionally classifies a parameter and checks overlap with a linear factor.

matches.rationale: Both convert linked logarithms into power equations, eliminate the intermediate variable through power-of-power substitutions, and return to the required logarithm base.
sharedKnowledge: Both convert linked logarithms into power equations, eliminate the intermediate variable through power-of-power substitutions, and return to the required logarithm base.

matches.rationale: Both track substituted logarithm bases through nested powers. The candidate additionally selects a valid proof order and distinguishes an exponent squared from a power squared.
sharedKnowledge: Both track substituted logarithm bases through nested powers. The candidate additionally selects a valid proof order and distinguishes an exponent squared from a power squared.

matches.rationale: Both require checking the original signs of sine and cosine. The original uses a reference right triangle and the stated quadrant to calculate their product. The follow-up diagnoses a lost sign when a principal square root is taken; it practises the sign check, but does not practise the reference-triangle calculation.

Both turn pairwise runner-order restrictions into complete permitted race orders. The original propagates those restrictions through position changes to a final order; the candidate fixes forced positions and counts the remaining permutations.
sharedKnowledge: Both turn pairwise runner-order restrictions into complete permitted race orders. The original propagates those restrictions through position changes to a final order; the candidate fixes forced positions and counts the remaining permutations.

matches.rationale: Both match similar triangles and convert ratios into an actual requested measure. The original obtains a scale from small-triangle perimeters and then area; the candidate converts diagonal part ratios to full-side scales and sums two lengths.
sharedKnowledge: Both match similar triangles and convert ratios into an actual requested measure. The original obtains a scale from small-triangle perimeters and then area; the candidate converts diagonal part ratios to full-side scales and sums two lengths.

matches.rationale: Both determine when a parameterised sum of nonnegative radicals has a real solution, preserving the zero-parameter case and proving sufficiency. The original uses a square/fourth-root minimum and then tests a sufficient subset; the official problem uses two square roots and asks for the full feasible set.
sharedKnowledge: Both determine when a parameterised sum of nonnegative radicals has a real solution, preserving the zero-parameter case and proving sufficiency. The original uses a square/fourth-root minimum and then tests a sufficient subset; the official problem uses two square roots and asks for the full feasible set.

matches.rationale: Both replace x² by a nonnegative variable and require two distinct positive quadratic roots to obtain four distinct original roots. The official problem varies both coefficients; the original then compares its exact interval with a necessary but insufficient superset.
sharedKnowledge: Both replace x² by a nonnegative variable and require two distinct positive quadratic roots to obtain four distinct original roots. The official problem varies both coefficients; the original then compares its exact interval with a necessary but insufficient superset.

matches.rationale: Both compare positive-base powers at positive and negative exponents, allowing the ordering to reverse across base one. The original checks simultaneous values for proposed rules; the candidate additionally finds attained extremes over a cosine range and solves a quadratic base condition.
sharedKnowledge: Both compare positive-base powers at positive and negative exponents, allowing the ordering to reverse across base one. The original checks simultaneous values for proposed rules; the candidate additionally finds attained extremes over a cosine range and solves a quadratic base condition.

matches.rationale: Both retain the possible nondegenerate SSA triangles and check where a second branch appears or collapses. The original uses sine-rule supplementary angles and the angle sum. The follow-up uses the perpendicular height and checks positive side lengths. These are different constructions for the same SSA boundary check.
sharedKnowledge: Both retain the possible nondegenerate SSA triangles and check where a second branch appears or collapses. The original uses sine-rule supplementary angles and the angle sum. The follow-up uses the perpendicular height and checks positive side lengths. These are different constructions for the same SSA boundary check.

matches.rationale: Both seek the complete parameter set giving exactly one nondegenerate SSA triangle, including a tangent case and the boundary where another configuration collapses.
sharedKnowledge: Both seek the complete parameter set giving exactly one nondegenerate SSA triangle, including a tangent case and the boundary where another configuration collapses.

matches.rationale: Both require retaining the two possible triangles in an SSA situation and rejecting degenerate cases. The original uses the sine rule and angle sums to find when exactly one triangle remains. The follow-up uses the cosine rule to find the two possible sides and compare areas. It practises recognising both SSA branches, with a different calculation afterwards.

Both use containments between listed input conditions and the exactly-one-answer rule to eliminate an option that would force another option true. The original additionally requires a sufficient condition to be nonnecessary.
sharedKnowledge: Both use containments between listed input conditions and the exactly-one-answer rule to eliminate an option that would force another option true. The original additionally requires a sufficient condition to be nonnecessary.

matches.rationale: Both interpret conditions as input sets and count which other conditions are logically forced by containment. The candidate asks for exactly three consequences, while the original identifies a uniquely proper sufficient subset of an unknown success set.
sharedKnowledge: Both interpret conditions as input sets and count which other conditions are logically forced by containment. The candidate asks for exactly three consequences, while the original identifies a uniquely proper sufficient subset of an unknown success set.

matches.rationale: Both evaluate multiple statements at one shared input and enforce an exact total of truths using equivalences/implications. The original has real inequalities and two truths; the candidate has a positive-integer count and one truth.

matches.rationale: Both combine full inequality assumptions to decide which whole sign claims are forced. The original exploits a truth-count restriction and absolute values; the candidate adds strict chains and uses counterexamples for an unsupported order.

matches.rationale: Both calculate the area of a horizontally compressed triangular wave by balancing each piece’s width with the number of repeated pieces. The original uses the resulting integral as a recurrence multiplier; the candidate sums several differently compressed terms.
sharedKnowledge: Both calculate the area of a horizontally compressed triangular wave by balancing each piece’s width with the number of repeated pieces. The original uses the resulting integral as a recurrence multiplier; the candidate sums several differently compressed terms.

matches.rationale: Both evaluate a definite integral to obtain the constant multiplier in a recurrence, then identify the resulting geometric behaviour with its correct initial index. The original additionally has a fractional-part integrand and asks about convergence of an infinite sum.
sharedKnowledge: Both evaluate a definite integral to obtain the constant multiplier in a recurrence, then identify the resulting geometric behaviour with its correct initial index. The original additionally has a fractional-part integrand and asks about convergence of an infinite sum.

matches.rationale: Both generate a deterministic recurrence until its full relevant state repeats, prove the cycle and align a distant index. The original uses ordered pairs of remainders and counts divisibility positions; the candidate uses one-term numerical states with a nonrepeating start.

matches.rationale: Both prove a minimum information requirement by asking whether different possible states remain indistinguishable after an observation, then construct a scheme meeting the bound. The original designs answer patterns that cannot be distinguished from four truth checks; the candidate designs one feedback trial that distinguishes the remaining password permutations.

matches.rationale: Both compare paired function arguments to identify a reflection centre and test whether an all-input condition is necessary/sufficient. The original first composes transformations and seeks a sufficient nonnecessary special rule; the candidate tests three general symmetry identities.

matches.rationale: Both write horizontal operations in order, equate the resulting functions and rename one input to obtain a universal identity. Different operation orders here lead to a periodic identity rather than the original reflection identity.

matches.rationale: Both split an absolute-value integrand at every sign breakpoint and preserve signed areas when recombining pieces. The original additionally follows an accumulated integral’s extrema and counts parameter-dependent roots; the candidate evaluates one fixed definite integral.

matches.rationale: Both translate sign-based universal rules into implications, group contrapositives, split an equivalence and use exactly one truth plus a consistent function. The original has seven differently directed rules and strict/non-strict boundaries; the official question has six, so this is a variant rather than a reprint.

matches.rationale: Both translate stationary points into real roots of a polynomial derivative and use factorisation to count them. The candidate is a prerequisite count with a quadratic factor; the original additionally classifies sign changes, counts multiplicities and constructs a degree-constrained configuration.

lessons.title: Solve quadratics and use their roots
knowledge: Solve quadratic equations by factorisation or the quadratic formula, retaining both signs.
Use the sum and product of roots to evaluate symmetric expressions.
Build a quadratic from its roots and check the requested quantity.

lessons.title: Use the quadratic boundary
knowledge: Complete the square with the leading coefficient accounted for.
Use the discriminant to distinguish two distinct, repeated and absent real roots.
Check a parameter value that removes the quadratic term separately.
Identify a quadratic minimum and conditions for positivity or no intersection.

lessons.title: Mark boundaries and test intervals
knowledge: Mark numerator zeros and excluded denominator values before testing interval signs.
Intersect simultaneous inequalities and retain the appropriate endpoints.
Interpret an absolute-value distance bound as an interval.
Do not multiply an inequality by an expression whose sign is unknown.

lessons.title: Use index laws and one common base
knowledge: Use positive-base index laws, including negative and fractional exponents.
Convert powers to a common positive base other than 1 before equating exponents.
Replace a repeated exponential by a positive variable and recover the original input with logarithms.

lessons.title: Combine logarithms before solving
knowledge: State positive logarithm arguments before combining logarithms.
Use product, quotient and power laws to convert a logarithmic equation into a power equation.
Reject candidates outside the original domain and undo any logarithmic substitution.

lessons.title: Read the ratio before summing
knowledge: Identify the signed common ratio by writing initial terms.
Use finite GP sums, including the ratio-one case, and check absolute ratio below one before summing infinitely.
Powers of GP terms produce corresponding powers of the first term and ratio.
In probability applications, retain the original equally likely sample space when filtering convergence.

lessons.title: Move the input and the height
knowledge: Find transformed points by equating the new inner expression to the old input, then transform the old height.
Interpret translations, stretches and reflections through their effect on input and output.
A negative output multiplier exchanges maxima and minima; successive transformations follow the stated order.

knowledge: Work with the whole trigonometric input to find periods, zeros and peaks.
Convert radians and degrees and use exact values for standard angles.
Sine and cosine have period 2π and range [−1,1]; tangent has period π and asymptotes π/2+kπ.
Use even cosine and odd sine/tangent symmetry; tangent as sine divided by cosine requires nonzero cosine.

knowledge: Transform the interval along with the trigonometric input and retain every branch in that interval.
Use sin²x+cos²x=1 to reduce an equation to one trigonometric function.
Factor instead of dividing away possible zero factors.
Check original signs after squaring; sqrt(a²)=|a| and denominator exclusions still apply.

lessons.title: Choose a rule and retain both triangles
knowledge: Choose sine or cosine rule according to the known sides and angles.
Retain both valid triangles in an SSA situation and reject degenerate or incompatible candidates.
Use the included angle in the triangle-area formula.
Identify the relevant plane before applying triangle rules in three dimensions.

lessons.title: Rewrite powers before differentiating
knowledge: Rewrite quotients, roots and products as sums of powers before differentiating.
Apply the power rule to rational exponents on the appropriate domain.
Differentiate twice before evaluating a requested second derivative.

lessons.title: Read the shape from derivative signs

Use derivative sign changes to classify local maxima and minima.
A zero derivative without a sign change need not be a local extreme.
Use the original function to find stationary-point heights.

lessons.title: Integrate powers, then use the missing information
knowledge: Simplify to powers before integrating and use the power rule except at exponent −1.
Include an integration constant and determine it from an initial value on the same interval; an excluded point can separate intervals with different constants.
Evaluate a definite integral as an antiderivative at the upper limit minus its value at the lower limit.

lessons.title: Separate signed accumulation from total area
knowledge: Distinguish a signed integral from total geometric area.
Find all intersections and integrate upper minus lower on each separate region.
Split when a curve crosses or an absolute-value formula changes.
The worked absolute-value example treats negative and nonnegative inputs separately.

lessons.title: Turn a ratio into an equation
knowledge: Convert a ratio of quantities into an equation before solving.
Name a repeated exponential as a positive variable to obtain a quadratic.
Reject nonpositive values of the substituted exponential and use its monotonicity to select the largest input.

lessons.title: Simplify lengths before finding an area
knowledge: Simplify square-root lengths using sqrt(z²)=|z| and the sign supplied by the geometric domain.
Express an area as a product of simplified lengths or as an outer area minus pieces.
Cancel shared side or angle factors when taking triangle-area ratios.

lessons.title: Find the allowed range before optimising
knowledge: Replace an inner expression by a variable with its allowed interval before optimising.
Compare both endpoints and any permitted quadratic vertex.
For a^cos(x) with a>0, the extreme values are a and 1/a and their separation is |a−1/a|.
Split the absolute-value equation into cases, multiply by positive a, and retain roots compatible with each case.

lessons.title: Use the two possible triangles
knowledge: Use a common triangle height to turn an area ratio into a side ratio.
Model the two possible side lengths as roots of one cosine-rule quadratic.
Compare root sums/products or subtract Pythagoras equations to eliminate a shared height.
For an acute given angle, compare the opposite side with the perpendicular height and adjacent side to count possible SSA triangles.

lessons.title: Rename a hidden variable
knowledge: Name an entire repeated expression to expose a simpler equation.
State the permitted values of a new squared, logarithmic or reciprocal variable and recover the original variable afterwards.
Write full binomial coefficients and compare their ratios to find a/b without finding both constants.
Distinguish ascending and descending term positions and apply case-defined functions only to allowed inputs.

lessons.title: Count roots from the turning heights
knowledge: Use derivative signs to divide a graph into monotonic pieces.
Evaluate turning heights on the original function to count axis crossings or intersections with a horizontal level.
Count a touching root once and use strict inequalities when distinct roots are required.
Check the positive half of the graph and its height at zero when counting positive roots.

lessons.title: Read the terms before choosing a sum
knowledge: Write initial terms and use the rule to distinguish a geometric progression from a periodic sequence.
A shift of k positions scales an equal-length GP block by r^k.
For an autonomous one-term recurrence u(n+1)=f(u(n)), a repeated value restarts the cycle; a recurrence depending on several terms or on n requires its full state and index phase to repeat.
Count inclusive endpoints, split periodic sums into complete cycles and a remainder, and check infinite-GP convergence.

lessons.title: Simplify surds and rationalise
knowledge: Extract square factors and combine like surds.
Multiply by a nonzero conjugate to rationalise a denominator.
Factor a difference of squares to simplify a surd quotient before calculus.
Keep sqrt(x²)=|x| and all original denominator exclusions.

lessons.title: Turn proportion into a multiplier
knowledge: Turn percentage changes into successive multipliers and divide by their product to recover an original amount.
Write direct or inverse proportionality using a fixed constant.
Translate ratios into fractions of a whole and use the correct length, area or volume scale.
Distinguish simple interest, compound growth and the order of deposits or withdrawals.

lessons.title: Differentiate an accumulated total
knowledge: For a continuous integrand, differentiate an accumulated integral with fixed lower bound and upper endpoint x by evaluating the integrand at x.
Reverse limits when the moving endpoint is the lower one.
Use signed integrals to calculate changes in the accumulated total.
Use integrand signs to classify extrema of the accumulated function and compare endpoints for an absolute maximum.

lessons.title: Read the domain, then AND, OR and NOT
knowledge: Fix the allowed inputs before deciding whether a statement is true.
AND requires both statements; inclusive OR permits either or both; NOT reverses the truth of the whole statement.
Negating a strict inequality includes its equality boundary.
Count whole true statements at the same input when exactly two or exactly one are required.
Some means at least one; not prime is not equivalent to composite because 1 is neither.

lessons.title: Translate IF and ONLY IF before reasoning
knowledge: Identify the premise and conclusion by rewriting a sentence as an if-then implication.
A if B means B implies A; A only if B means A implies B.
If and only if requires both implication directions.
An implication fails precisely when its premise is true and its conclusion false; a false premise is not a counterexample.
A restriction on selected objects need not require any objects to be selected.

lessons.title: Reverse and negate for the contrapositive
knowledge: The converse reverses an implication and needs its own justification.
The contrapositive reverses and negates both clauses and is equivalent to the original implication.
A true premise forces its conclusion, and a false conclusion forces a false premise.
Knowing the conclusion alone does not establish the premise; denying the premise does not deny the conclusion.
Chains of implications can rule out statements as the sole true statement.

lessons.title: Test NECESSARY and SUFFICIENT separately
knowledge: Keep the target fixed: sufficiency tests condition implies target, while necessity tests target implies condition.
Classify a condition by proving each successful direction and giving an allowed counterexample for each failed direction.
Necessary and sufficient describes both directions, as in an if-and-only-if condition.
A stronger condition may be sufficient without being necessary.
For ax+by=c with nonzero coefficients, gradient and intercept signs are determined by -a/b and c/b.

lessons.title: Who is chosen first: EVERY or SOME?
knowledge: Every quantifies over all allowed inputs; there exists requires at least one allowed witness.
Read nested choices in order: a later witness may depend on an earlier input.
One fixed witness working for all inputs is a stronger requirement than choosing a witness separately for each input.
Construct a witness to prove existence and choose a defeating input to disprove a proposed fixed universal witness.
The same existence statement may change truth when its domain changes from integers to reals.

lessons.title: Negate the whole claim, keeping the domain
knowledge: Negate from the outer quantifier inward, swapping every and there exists without changing their order or domains.
The failure of a universal statement is one allowed counterexample; the failure of existence means all allowed candidates fail.
Negating AND gives an OR of negations, while negating OR gives an AND of negations.
To negate an implication, require its premise and the negation of its conclusion.
An if-and-only-if statement fails when exactly one of its two conditions is true; preserve equality when negating inequalities.

lessons.title: Disprove a claim with one allowed example
knowledge: A counterexample must satisfy every hypothesis and violate the conclusion.
For an implication, a true premise and false conclusion are both required.
One counterexample disproves an always-claim, while many successful cases do not prove it.
Check divisibility and primality against their definitions when choosing an integer counterexample.
Negative real inputs can defeat claims that squaring preserves order.

lessons.title: Cover every case
knowledge: Choose cases that exhaust the stated domain and prove the claim in every case.
Even and odd cases include all integers, including zero and negative integers.
Use |x|=x for x>=0 and |x|=-x for x<0; assign boundary points to a case.
Integer squares leave remainder 0 or 1 modulo 4, as shown by parity cases.
For sums of absolute values, split at each point where an inner expression changes sign.

lessons.title: Put each reason before the step that needs it
knowledge: Order a proof by dependencies: a line may use the hypotheses and previously justified lines.
Introduce symbols before using them and establish nonzero denominators before dividing.
Independent justified lines can sometimes be interchanged.
Translate a logarithm definition into a power and use exponent laws to connect a chain of equalities.

lessons.title: Find the first unsupported step
knowledge: Check each inference using only the assumptions and earlier justified lines, and stop at the first unsupported step.
A true conclusion does not make an invalid or incomplete proof correct.
Circular reasoning assumes the conclusion that the proof is meant to establish.
Dividing by an expression that may vanish can lose a solution; rearrangement and factorisation retain that case.
Squaring is valid forwards, but its candidate roots must be checked in the original equation.

lessons.title: Check what division loses and squaring adds
knowledge: Before cancelling an expression, check and handle the case where it equals zero.
Rearranging to a zero product can preserve solutions that division would discard.
Squaring an equality gives a necessary condition, but the squared equation may contain additional candidate roots.
Substitute candidates back into the original equation, respecting the nonnegative square root.
Equal function outputs need not imply equal inputs, as with squares and supplementary sine values.

lessons.title: Track signs before using an algebraic rule
knowledge: Multiplication or division by a negative number reverses an inequality.
An unknown multiplier sign may require positive, negative and zero cases.
For c>0, |z|>=c means z<=-c or z>=c, including both equality endpoints.
The zero-product rule requires a product equal to zero; a nonzero product does not fix individual factors.
Use the stated signs to bound ratios of negative numbers.

lessons.title: Observe a cycle, then prove the rule repeats it
knowledge: Initial terms suggest a cycle; the recurrence must establish return to the same state.
When a recurrence depends on the index, the index phase must also repeat.
Find a distant term from its position within a proved repeating block.
Compute a long sum using complete blocks and leftover terms.
Repeating terms need not give repeating partial sums when a whole block has nonzero sum; a finite list without a rule does not force its continuation.

lessons.title: Use geometry to test a universal claim
knowledge: Translate a geometric condition into lengths, areas or angles before deciding what it forces.
Triangle area with two sides and the included angle is half the product of the sides and the sine of that angle.
For angles strictly between 0 and 180 degrees, equal sine allows equal or supplementary angles.
A nonsquare rectangle inscribed in a circle gives equal centre-to-side triangle areas without regularity.
A symmetric example proves possibility, while a universal symmetry claim needs proof or an allowed irregular counterexample.

lessons.title: Combine conditions before choosing
knowledge: Exactly one requires one entire statement to hold and all others to fail.
Use shared inputs and implications between listed statements to exclude statements that would force another truth.
Equivalent statements, including a statement and its contrapositive, have matching truth values.
A guarantee over a larger input set implies the same guarantee over each contained smaller set.
An iff fails in the two cases where exactly one component is true; different false universal rules may fail at different inputs.
After identifying the sole possible true rule, construct a consistent example if needed.

lessons.title: Complete each stage of a proof
knowledge: Existence needs an allowed solution; uniqueness needs proof that every solution equals that candidate.
A necessary candidate condition must be completed by substitution in the original problem or by reversible steps.
A contradiction proof retains the original assumptions, denies the target and finishes with explicitly incompatible facts.
Order definitions and conditions before proof lines that use them.
Rewrite logarithm definitions as powers and regroup exponents to connect a longer chain without assuming its conclusion.
Equal products do not force equality of corresponding factors.

lessons.title: Integer cases and supplied definitions
knowledge: Cover every possible remainder modulo a positive integer to prove a divisibility or remainder claim.
A prime divisible by another prime must equal that prime, so check the prime itself before declaring a multiple composite.
Products of consecutive integers provide small factors; divisibility by 2 and 3 ensures divisibility by 6, but overlapping factors cannot be counted twice.
For a supplied definition, preserve the order of member, factor and partner choices, allowing later choices to depend on earlier ones.
Negating every member has a suitable choice means one member has no suitable choice.
Keep other-member restrictions explicit: self-divisibility cannot supply a different partner.

lessons.title: Use an identity at useful inputs
knowledge: An identity holds at every allowed input; useful substitutions can make function arguments coincide or produce simultaneous equations.
Opposite heights equally spaced around a centre imply a zero value at that centre and signed integral cancellation on intervals with that midpoint.
Symmetry about one centre does not guarantee cancellation on an interval with a different midpoint.
Write the transformed input for each graph operation, then compare the two operation orders.
An identity f(x+T)=f(x) establishes a period, not necessarily the smallest positive period; positive integer multiples are also periods.
Replacing x by -x reflects roots and exchanges their positive and negative signs.

lessons.title: Find the full parameter range
knowledge: Check parameter values at which an equation changes degree before using a quadratic discriminant or dividing by a coefficient.
A nondegenerate quadratic has two distinct real roots for positive discriminant and one distinct repeated root for zero discriminant.
The substitution u=x^2 retains u>=0: positive u gives two real x values, zero gives one and negative u gives none.
Two distinct positive roots of the quadratic in u are needed for four distinct real roots of an even quartic; use discriminant, root sum and product.
Use cubic turning heights to classify real-root counts and inspect zero turning heights at parameter boundaries.
Prove the full necessary-and-sufficient range; a narrower sufficient condition alone does not describe all successful parameters.

lessons.title: Prove a bound and attain it
knowledge: An extremal solution requires a bound excluding every better value and a construction attaining that bound.
Round a lower bound on an integer count upward, then check that the proposed arrangement works.
Circular chair coverage requires checking the wrap-around gap as well as internal gaps.
Sort data to use medians, range and mean constraints; bound the total in terms of the median and then build an attaining list.
For a sorted triple with mean mu and median m, the two outer entries sum to 3mu-m.
Distinctness applies across the full construction, including separate triples; case splits can be needed to prove the least overall range.

lessons.title: Justify what a recurrence preserves
knowledge: Prove that a recurrence update preserves a property, then use the initial state to justify repeated application.
The update (x,y) to (y,x+y) preserves the full set of common divisors by addition forwards and subtraction backwards, so adjacent HCFs agree.
A property proved for adjacent terms need not hold for separated terms.
A two-term recurrence needs a repeated ordered pair to restart the process; repeating parity states need not mean repeating numerical values.
Prove that an interval bound survives the next update to control distant terms without a closed formula.
Separate a non-repeating start from a later cycle and count from the actual cycle start; periodic sums still require leftover-block checks.

lessons.title: Test claims about whole functions
knowledge: A functional counterexample must satisfy the hypothesis everywhere on the required domain or interval.
Increasing function height does not imply increasing gradient, and positive height does not imply positive gradient.
An integral of a square is nonnegative, while an ordinary signed integral may cancel.

On a nonempty forward interval, subtract shared integration intervals to isolate a sign constraint; for a continuous function, a nonpositive integral forces at least one nonpositive value, not nonpositivity everywhere.
The distinct roots of a product are the combined roots of its factors, with overlaps counted once.
A nonzero cubic has opposite-sign tails and cannot be positive on the entire real line.

lessons.title: Integrate powers, then use the missing information
knowledge: Simplify to powers before integrating and use the power rule except at exponent −1.
Include an integration constant and determine it from an initial value on the same interval; an excluded point can separate intervals with different constants.
Evaluate a definite integral as an antiderivative at the upper limit minus its value at the lower limit.

lessons.title: Separate signed accumulation from total area
knowledge: Distinguish a signed integral from total geometric area.
Find all intersections and integrate upper minus lower on each separate region.
Split when a curve crosses or an absolute-value formula changes.
The worked absolute-value example treats negative and nonnegative inputs separately.

lessons.title: Turn a ratio into an equation
knowledge: Convert a ratio of quantities into an equation before solving.
Name a repeated exponential as a positive variable to obtain a quadratic.
Reject nonpositive values of the substituted exponential and use its monotonicity to select the largest input.

lessons.title: Simplify lengths before finding an area
knowledge: Simplify square-root lengths using sqrt(z²)=|z| and the sign supplied by the geometric domain.
Express an area as a product of simplified lengths or as an outer area minus pieces.
Cancel shared side or angle factors when taking triangle-area ratios.

lessons.title: Find the allowed range before optimising
knowledge: Replace an inner expression by a variable with its allowed interval before optimising.
Compare both endpoints and any permitted quadratic vertex.
For a^cos(x) with a>0, the extreme values are a and 1/a and their separation is |a−1/a|.
Split the absolute-value equation into cases, multiply by positive a, and retain roots compatible with each case.

lessons.title: Use the two possible triangles
knowledge: Use a common triangle height to turn an area ratio into a side ratio.
Model the two possible side lengths as roots of one cosine-rule quadratic.
Compare root sums/products or subtract Pythagoras equations to eliminate a shared height.
For an acute given angle, compare the opposite side with the perpendicular height and adjacent side to count possible SSA triangles.

lessons.title: Rename a hidden variable
knowledge: Name an entire repeated expression to expose a simpler equation.
State the permitted values of a new squared, logarithmic or reciprocal variable and recover the original variable afterwards.
Write full binomial coefficients and compare their ratios to find a/b without finding both constants.
Distinguish ascending and descending term positions and apply case-defined functions only to allowed inputs.

lessons.title: Count roots from the turning heights
knowledge: Use derivative signs to divide a graph into monotonic pieces.
Evaluate turning heights on the original function to count axis crossings or intersections with a horizontal level.
Count a touching root once and use strict inequalities when distinct roots are required.
Check the positive half of the graph and its height at zero when counting positive roots.

lessons.title: Read the terms before choosing a sum
knowledge: Write initial terms and use the rule to distinguish a geometric progression from a periodic sequence.
A shift of k positions scales an equal-length GP block by r^k.
For an autonomous one-term recurrence u(n+1)=f(u(n)), a repeated value restarts the cycle; a recurrence depending on several terms or on n requires its full state and index phase to repeat.
Count inclusive endpoints, split periodic sums into complete cycles and a remainder, and check infinite-GP convergence.

lessons.title: Simplify surds and rationalise
knowledge: Extract square factors and combine like surds.
Multiply by a nonzero conjugate to rationalise a denominator.
Factor a difference of squares to simplify a surd quotient before calculus.
Keep sqrt(x²)=|x| and all original denominator exclusions.

lessons.title: Turn proportion into a multiplier
knowledge: Turn percentage changes into successive multipliers and divide by their product to recover an original amount.
Write direct or inverse proportionality using a fixed constant.
Translate ratios into fractions of a whole and use the correct length, area or volume scale.
Distinguish simple interest, compound growth and the order of deposits or withdrawals.

lessons.title: Differentiate an accumulated total
knowledge: For a continuous integrand, differentiate an accumulated integral with fixed lower bound and upper endpoint x by evaluating the integrand at x.
Reverse limits when the moving endpoint is the lower one.
Use signed integrals to calculate changes in the accumulated total.
Use integrand signs to classify extrema of the accumulated function and compare endpoints for an absolute maximum.

lessons.title: Read the domain, then AND, OR and NOT
knowledge: Fix the allowed inputs before deciding whether a statement is true.
AND requires both statements; inclusive OR permits either or both; NOT reverses the truth of the whole statement.
Negating a strict inequality includes its equality boundary.
Count whole true statements at the same input when exactly two or exactly one are required.
Some means at least one; not prime is not equivalent to composite because 1 is neither.

lessons.title: Translate IF and ONLY IF before reasoning
knowledge: Identify the premise and conclusion by rewriting a sentence as an if-then implication.
A if B means B implies A; A only if B means A implies B.
If and only if requires both implication directions.
An implication fails precisely when its premise is true and its conclusion false; a false premise is not a counterexample.
A restriction on selected objects need not require any objects to be selected.

lessons.title: Reverse and negate for the contrapositive
knowledge: The converse reverses an implication and needs its own justification.
The contrapositive reverses and negates both clauses and is equivalent to the original implication.
A true premise forces its conclusion, and a false conclusion forces a false premise.
Knowing the conclusion alone does not establish the premise; denying the premise does not deny the conclusion.
Chains of implications can rule out statements as the sole true statement.

lessons.title: Test NECESSARY and SUFFICIENT separately
knowledge: Keep the target fixed: sufficiency tests condition implies target, while necessity tests target implies condition.
Classify a condition by proving each successful direction and giving an allowed counterexample for each failed direction.
Necessary and sufficient describes both directions, as in an if-and-only-if condition.
A stronger condition may be sufficient without being necessary.
For ax+by=c with nonzero coefficients, gradient and intercept signs are determined by -a/b and c/b.

lessons.title: Who is chosen first: EVERY or SOME?
knowledge: Every quantifies over all allowed inputs; there exists requires at least one allowed witness.
Read nested choices in order: a later witness may depend on an earlier input.
One fixed witness working for all inputs is a stronger requirement than choosing a witness separately for each input.
Construct a witness to prove existence and choose a defeating input to disprove a proposed fixed universal witness.
The same existence statement may change truth when its domain changes from integers to reals.

lessons.title: Negate the whole claim, keeping the domain
knowledge: Negate from the outer quantifier inward, swapping every and there exists without changing their order or domains.
The failure of a universal statement is one allowed counterexample; the failure of existence means all allowed candidates fail.
Negating AND gives an OR of negations, while negating OR gives an AND of negations.
To negate an implication, require its premise and the negation of its conclusion.
An if-and-only-if statement fails when exactly one of its two conditions is true; preserve equality when negating inequalities.

lessons.title: Disprove a claim with one allowed example
knowledge: A counterexample must satisfy every hypothesis and violate the conclusion.
For an implication, a true premise and false conclusion are both required.
One counterexample disproves an always-claim, while many successful cases do not prove it.
Check divisibility and primality against their definitions when choosing an integer counterexample.
Negative real inputs can defeat claims that squaring preserves order.

lessons.title: Cover every case
knowledge: Choose cases that exhaust the stated domain and prove the claim in every case.
Even and odd cases include all integers, including zero and negative integers.
Use |x|=x for x>=0 and |x|=-x for x<0; assign boundary points to a case.
Integer squares leave remainder 0 or 1 modulo 4, as shown by parity cases.
For sums of absolute values, split at each point where an inner expression changes sign.

lessons.title: Put each reason before the step that needs it
knowledge: Order a proof by dependencies: a line may use the hypotheses and previously justified lines.
Introduce symbols before using them and establish nonzero denominators before dividing.
Independent justified lines can sometimes be interchanged.
Translate a logarithm definition into a power and use exponent laws to connect a chain of equalities.

lessons.title: Find the first unsupported step
knowledge: Check each inference using only the assumptions and earlier justified lines, and stop at the first unsupported step.
A true conclusion does not make an invalid or incomplete proof correct.
Circular reasoning assumes the conclusion that the proof is meant to establish.
Dividing by an expression that may vanish can lose a solution; rearrangement and factorisation retain that case.
Squaring is valid forwards, but its candidate roots must be checked in the original equation.

lessons.title: Check what division loses and squaring adds
knowledge: Before cancelling an expression, check and handle the case where it equals zero.
Rearranging to a zero product can preserve solutions that division would discard.
Squaring an equality gives a necessary condition, but the squared equation may contain additional candidate roots.
Substitute candidates back into the original equation, respecting the nonnegative square root.
Equal function outputs need not imply equal inputs, as with squares and supplementary sine values.

lessons.title: Track signs before using an algebraic rule
knowledge: Multiplication or division by a negative number reverses an inequality.
An unknown multiplier sign may require positive, negative and zero cases.
For c>0, |z|>=c means z<=-c or z>=c, including both equality endpoints.
The zero-product rule requires a product equal to zero; a nonzero product does not fix individual factors.
Use the stated signs to bound ratios of negative numbers.

lessons.title: Observe a cycle, then prove the rule repeats it
knowledge: Initial terms suggest a cycle; the recurrence must establish return to the same state.
When a recurrence depends on the index, the index phase must also repeat.
Find a distant term from its position within a proved repeating block.
Compute a long sum using complete blocks and leftover terms.
Repeating terms need not give repeating partial sums when a whole block has nonzero sum; a finite list without a rule does not force its continuation.

lessons.title: Use geometry to test a universal claim
knowledge: Translate a geometric condition into lengths, areas or angles before deciding what it forces.
Triangle area with two sides and the included angle is half the product of the sides and the sine of that angle.
For angles strictly between 0 and 180 degrees, equal sine allows equal or supplementary angles.
A nonsquare rectangle inscribed in a circle gives equal centre-to-side triangle areas without regularity.
A symmetric example proves possibility, while a universal symmetry claim needs proof or an allowed irregular counterexample.

lessons.title: Combine conditions before choosing
knowledge: Exactly one requires one entire statement to hold and all others to fail.
Use shared inputs and implications between listed statements to exclude statements that would force another truth.
Equivalent statements, including a statement and its contrapositive, have matching truth values.
A guarantee over a larger input set implies the same guarantee over each contained smaller set.
An iff fails in the two cases where exactly one component is true; different false universal rules may fail at different inputs.
After identifying the sole possible true rule, construct a consistent example if needed.

lessons.title: Complete each stage of a proof
knowledge: Existence needs an allowed solution; uniqueness needs proof that every solution equals that candidate.
A necessary candidate condition must be completed by substitution in the original problem or by reversible steps.
A contradiction proof retains the original assumptions, denies the target and finishes with explicitly incompatible facts.
Order definitions and conditions before proof lines that use them.
Rewrite logarithm definitions as powers and regroup exponents to connect a longer chain without assuming its conclusion.
Equal products do not force equality of corresponding factors.

lessons.title: Integer cases and supplied definitions
knowledge: Cover every possible remainder modulo a positive integer to prove a divisibility or remainder claim.
A prime divisible by another prime must equal that prime, so check the prime itself before declaring a multiple composite.
Products of consecutive integers provide small factors; divisibility by 2 and 3 ensures divisibility by 6, but overlapping factors cannot be counted twice.
For a supplied definition, preserve the order of member, factor and partner choices, allowing later choices to depend on earlier ones.
Negating every member has a suitable choice means one member has no suitable choice.
Keep other-member restrictions explicit: self-divisibility cannot supply a different partner.

lessons.title: Use an identity at useful inputs
knowledge: An identity holds at every allowed input; useful substitutions can make function arguments coincide or produce simultaneous equations.
Opposite heights equally spaced around a centre imply a zero value at that centre and signed integral cancellation on intervals with that midpoint.
Symmetry about one centre does not guarantee cancellation on an interval with a different midpoint.
Write the transformed input for each graph operation, then compare the two operation orders.
An identity f(x+T)=f(x) establishes a period, not necessarily the smallest positive period; positive integer multiples are also periods.
Replacing x by -x reflects roots and exchanges their positive and negative signs.

lessons.title: Find the full parameter range
knowledge: Check parameter values at which an equation changes degree before using a quadratic discriminant or dividing by a coefficient.
A nondegenerate quadratic has two distinct real roots for positive discriminant and one distinct repeated root for zero discriminant.
The substitution u=x^2 retains u>=0: positive u gives two real x values, zero gives one and negative u gives none.
Two distinct positive roots of the quadratic in u are needed for four distinct real roots of an even quartic; use discriminant, root sum and product.
Use cubic turning heights to classify real-root counts and inspect zero turning heights at parameter boundaries.
Prove the full necessary-and-sufficient range; a narrower sufficient condition alone does not describe all successful parameters.

lessons.title: Prove a bound and attain it
knowledge: An extremal solution requires a bound excluding every better value and a construction attaining that bound.
Round a lower bound on an integer count upward, then check that the proposed arrangement works.
Circular chair coverage requires checking the wrap-around gap as well as internal gaps.
Sort data to use medians, range and mean constraints; bound the total in terms of the median and then build an attaining list.
For a sorted triple with mean mu and median m, the two outer entries sum to 3mu-m.
Distinctness applies across the full construction, including separate triples; case splits can be needed to prove the least overall range.

lessons.title: Justify what a recurrence preserves
knowledge: Prove that a recurrence update preserves a property, then use the initial state to justify repeated application.
The update (x,y) to (y,x+y) preserves the full set of common divisors by addition forwards and subtraction backwards, so adjacent HCFs agree.
A property proved for adjacent terms need not hold for separated terms.
A two-term recurrence needs a repeated ordered pair to restart the process; repeating parity states need not mean repeating numerical values.
Prove that an interval bound survives the next update to control distant terms without a closed formula.
Separate a non-repeating start from a later cycle and count from the actual cycle start; periodic sums still require leftover-block checks.

lessons.title: Test claims about whole functions
knowledge: A functional counterexample must satisfy the hypothesis everywhere on the required domain or interval.
Increasing function height does not imply increasing gradient, and positive height does not imply positive gradient.
An integral of a square is nonnegative, while an ordinary signed integral may cancel.

On a nonempty forward interval, subtract shared integration intervals to isolate a sign constraint; for a continuous function, a nonpositive integral forces at least one nonpositive value, not nonpositivity everywhere.
The distinct roots of a product are the combined roots of its factors, with overlaps counted once.
A nonzero cubic has opposite-sign tails and cannot be positive on the entire real line.

additionalConcepts.title: Recognise exponential and logarithmic graphs
knowledge: For \(a>0\), the graph of \(y=a^x\) has positive outputs and passes through \((0,1)\) and \((1,a)\).
For \(a>1\) the exponential increases, while for \(0<a<1\) it decreases; in each case \(y=0\) is a horizontal asymptote, whereas \(a=1\) gives the constant graph \(y=1\).
For \(a>0\) and \(a\ne1\), \(y=\log_a x\) has domain \(x>0\), passes through \((1,0)\) and \((a,1)\), and has vertical asymptote \(x=0\).
A logarithm increases for \(a>1\) and decreases for \(0<a<1\), so applying a decreasing logarithm reverses an inequality.
The graphs of \(y=a^x\) and \(y=\log_a x\) are reflections in \(y=x\) because their inputs and outputs are interchanged.

references.label: TMUA 2026 specification · MM5.1, MM5.2, MM8.1, M4.12

example.question: Which standard exponential or logarithmic graph has domain \(x>0\), decreases, passes through \((1,0)\) and \((\tfrac12,1)\), and has vertical asymptote \(x=0\)?
steps: The domain and vertical asymptote match a logarithm, rather than an exponential.
For \(y=\log_a x\), the point \((a,1)\) identifies the base, giving \(a=\tfrac12\).
The base lies between 0 and 1, consistent with the graph decreasing.

additionalConcepts.pitfall: A positive exponential base does not always give an increasing graph; bases between 0 and 1 reverse the direction.

additionalConcepts.title: Recognise square-root and reciprocal graphs
knowledge: The graph of \(y=\sqrt{x}\) starts at \((0,0)\), has domain and range \([0,\infty)\), and passes through \((1,1)\), \((4,2)\) and \((9,3)\).
The square-root graph increases and becomes less steep; it is the reflection of the \(x\ge0\) half of \(y=x^2\) in \(y=x\).
The graph of \(y=1/x\) has domain \(x\ne0\), range \(y\ne0\), and the two axes as asymptotes.
The reciprocal graph has branches in the first and third quadrants and decreases on each side of zero; it never joins across the excluded input.
Use key points, domains and asymptotes together, then apply any stated translations, stretches or reflections.

example.question: For \(y=1/(x-2)+1\), find the asymptotes and the intercepts with the coordinate axes.
steps: Translating \(y=1/x\) two units right and one up gives asymptotes \(x=2\) and \(y=1\).
For the y-intercept set \(x=0\): \(y=-1/2+1=1/2\).
For the x-intercept set \(y=0\): \(1/(x-2)=-1\), hence \(x=1\).

additionalConcepts.pitfall: For a square-root graph retain only the nonnegative root; for a reciprocal graph retain its excluded input.

additionalConcepts.title: Give each allowed input exactly one output
knowledge: A function assigns exactly one output to each input in its domain; different inputs may share the same output.
A one-to-one function has different outputs for different inputs, while a many-to-one function repeats at least one output.
A graph represents a function of x only if each vertical line meets it at most once, with every allowed input assigned a value.
The notation \(\sqrt{x}\) means the nonnegative square root: \(\sqrt9=3\), although solving \(u^2=9\) gives \(u=\pm3\).
The modulus \(|x|\) is distance from zero, so it equals \(x\) for \(x\ge0\) and \(-x\) for \(x<0\); in particular \(\sqrt{x^2}=|x|\).

example.question: Does \(y^2=x\) define y as a function of x on \(x\ge0\)? What changes for \(y=\sqrt{x}\)?
steps: At \(x=4\), the relation \(y^2=x\) allows both \(y=2\) and \(y=-2\).
One allowed input has two outputs, so this relation does not define a function of x.
The rule \(y=\sqrt{x}\) selects only the nonnegative output, giving exactly one output for each \(x\ge0\).
example.answer: \(y^2=x\) is not a function of x on this domain; \(y=\sqrt{x}\) is.

additionalConcepts.pitfall: Many inputs giving one output is allowed; one input giving several outputs is not a function.

additionalConcepts.title: Use angle facts, parallel lines and polygon sums
knowledge: Angles around a point total \(360^\circ\), angles on a straight line total \(180^\circ\), and perpendicular lines form \(90^\circ\) angles.
Vertically opposite angles at the intersection of two straight lines are equal.
When a transversal crosses parallel lines, corresponding angles and alternate angles are equal, while co-interior angles total \(180^\circ\).
A triangle has interior-angle sum \(180^\circ\), a quadrilateral has sum \(360^\circ\), and a triangle’s exterior angle equals the sum of its two opposite interior angles.

A simple \(n\)-sided polygon has interior-angle sum \((n-2)180^\circ\); the exterior turning angles of a convex polygon total \(360^\circ\), so a regular polygon has exterior angle \(360^\circ/n\) and interior angle \(180^\circ-360^\circ/n\).

example.question: A regular polygon has interior angle \(150^\circ\); how many sides does it have?
steps: An interior angle and its adjacent exterior angle lie on a straight line, so the exterior angle is \(180^\circ-150^\circ=30^\circ\).
The exterior angles total \(360^\circ\), and all are equal because the polygon is regular.
The number of sides is \(360/30=12\).

additionalConcepts.pitfall: Equal corresponding or alternate angles require parallel lines; a diagram that merely looks parallel is not enough.

additionalConcepts.title: Label the sides before using right-triangle ratios
knowledge: In a right-angled triangle, the hypotenuse is opposite the right angle; opposite and adjacent are named relative to the chosen acute angle \(\theta\), with adjacent excluding the hypotenuse.
The ratios are \(\sin\theta=\text{opposite}/\text{hypotenuse}\), \(\cos\theta=\text{adjacent}/\text{hypotenuse}\), and \(\tan\theta=\text{opposite}/\text{adjacent}\).
Pythagoras gives \(a^2+b^2=c^2\) when \(c\) is the hypotenuse; rearrange a ratio to find a length or identify an angle from its known exact ratio.
For a general triangle, a perpendicular height can create right triangles; in three dimensions, select the correct face, cross-section or projection before applying the same rules.

example.question: A right-angled triangle has sides of length \(6\), \(8\) and \(10\), with \(\theta\) opposite the side of length \(6\); find \(\sin\theta\), \(\cos\theta\) and \(\tan\theta\).
steps: The hypotenuse is \(10\), and \(6^2+8^2=10^2\) confirms the right triangle.
Relative to \(\theta\), the opposite side is \(6\) and the adjacent side is \(8\).
Therefore \(\sin\theta=6/10\), \(\cos\theta=8/10\), and \(\tan\theta=6/8\).

additionalConcepts.pitfall: Opposite and adjacent swap when you change the chosen acute angle; the hypotenuse never changes.

additionalConcepts.title: Match corresponding sides in similar triangles
knowledge: Similar triangles have equal corresponding angles and one common positive scale factor between corresponding side lengths.
Two equal angle pairs establish triangle similarity because the third angles must also agree. Name the correspondence before writing ratios.
Parallel lines often create equal corresponding or alternate angles and therefore similar triangles; justify those angles before using a scale factor.
For corresponding length ratio \(k\), similar figures have area ratio \(k^2\), and similar solids have volume ratio \(k^3\).
Equal area alone does not make triangles similar. Conversely, similar triangles of equal positive area have scale factor one and are congruent.

references.label: TMUA specification: M3.10, M5.5 and M5.17

example.question: In triangle ABC, P lies on AB and Q lies on AC, with PQ parallel to BC. Given \(AP=4\), \(AB=10\) and \(AC=15\), find AQ and the ratio of the areas of APQ and ABC.
steps: The parallel lines give equal corresponding angles, so triangles APQ and ABC are similar, with A matching A, P matching B and Q matching C.
The length scale from ABC to APQ is \(AP/AB=4/10=2/5\). Thus \(AQ=(2/5)\times15=6\).
The area ratio is the square of the length ratio: \((2/5)^2=4/25\).

additionalConcepts.pitfall: Keep corresponding sides in the same order in every ratio. A length scale factor is squared for area, not used unchanged.

additionalConcepts.title: Count polynomial roots from signs and degree
knowledge: A polynomial graph is continuous. If its values at two inputs have opposite signs, it must cross the horizontal axis at least once between them.
Values of the same sign do not rule out roots between them: the graph may cross twice or touch the axis. Check separately whether an endpoint itself is a root.
A nonzero polynomial of degree \(n\) has at most \(n\) distinct real roots. A repeated root counts only once when the question asks for distinct roots.
For sufficiently large positive or negative inputs, the leading term determines the sign. Use its coefficient and whether its degree is odd or even to establish the two tails.
Find disjoint intervals that each contain a root, then compare this lower bound with the degree's upper bound. When these bounds agree, the root count is exact.

example.question: Show that \(f(x)=x^3-4x\) has exactly three distinct real roots by considering signs and degree.
steps: There is a sign change on each of \((-3,-1)\), \((-1,1)\) and \((1,3)\). Continuity gives at least one root in each of these disjoint intervals, so at least three distinct roots.
The polynomial is a nonzero cubic, so it has at most three distinct real roots. Therefore it has exactly three.
As a check, \(x^3-4x=x(x-2)(x+2)\), giving the three roots \(-2,0,2\).

additionalConcepts.pitfall: A sign change proves at least one root, not exactly one. Do not conclude there are no roots between two values of the same sign.

additionalConcepts.title: Use repeated factors to predict polynomial signs
knowledge: If a polynomial has the factor \((x-r)^m\) and its remaining factor is nonzero at \(r\), the positive integer \(m\) is the root multiplicity. The remaining factor keeps the same sign sufficiently near \(r\).
An odd power of \(x-r\) changes sign across \(r\); an even power does not. Thus odd-multiplicity roots cross the axis, while even-multiplicity roots touch it without crossing.

The sum of the multiplicities of distinct real roots cannot exceed the degree of a nonzero polynomial. Count a repeated root once as a location but with all its repeated factors when using the degree.

Applied to a polynomial derivative, this sign test distinguishes a zero where the original function turns from a zero where it continues in the same direction. Use the derivative signs to decide maximum or minimum.

example.question: For \(p(x)=(x+1)^2(x-2)\), decide whether the graph crosses the axis at each real root.
steps: The distinct roots are \(-1\) and \(2\), with multiplicities 2 and 1.
Near \(-1\), the factor \(x-2\) is negative on both sides and the square is positive away from the root, so the sign does not change.
Near \(2\), the square remains positive while \(x-2\) changes sign, so the graph crosses there.
example.answer: It touches at \(x=-1\) and crosses at \(x=2\).

additionalConcepts.pitfall: Distinct-root counts and factor multiplicities answer different questions. A stationary input is not automatically a local maximum or minimum.
